title: Periodicity
lead: The representative elements divide into metals, metalloids and nonmetals by their places in the periodic table. The representative metals are taken group by group, from the alkali metals through groups 2, 12, 13 and 14 to bismuth in group 15, with how readily each reacts, the ions each forms and the films that protect them.
objectives: Make predictions about the periodicity properties of the representative elements
summary_html: This section focuses on the periodicity of the representative elements. These are the elements where the electrons are entering the s and p orbitals. The representative elements occur in groups 1, 2, and 12–18. These elements are representative metals, metalloids, and nonmetals. The alkali metals (group 1) are very reactive, readily form ions with a charge of 1+ to form ionic compounds that are usually soluble in water, and react vigorously with water to form hydrogen gas and a basic solution of the metal hydroxide. The outermost electrons of the alkaline earth metals (group 2) are more difficult to remove than the outer electron of the alkali metals, leading to the group 2 metals being less reactive than those in group 1. These elements easily form compounds in which the metals exhibit an oxidation state of 2+. Zinc, cadmium, and mercury (group 12) commonly exhibit the group oxidation state of 2+ (although mercury also exhibits an oxidation state of 1+ in compounds that contain ${\text{Hg}}_{2}{}^{2+}).$ Aluminum, gallium, indium, and thallium (group 13) are easier to oxidize than is hydrogen. Aluminum, gallium, and indium occur with an oxidation state 3+ (however, thallium also commonly occurs as the Tl+ ion). Tin and lead form stable divalent cations and covalent compounds in which the metals exhibit the 4+-oxidation state.

exercises.prompt: How do alkali metals differ from alkaline earth metals in atomic structure and general properties?

answer.solution: The alkali metals all have a single s electron in their outermost shell. In contrast, the alkaline earth metals have a completed s subshell in their outermost shell. In general, the alkali metals react faster and are more reactive than the corresponding alkaline earth metals in the same period.

exercises.prompt: Why does the reactivity of the alkali metals decrease from cesium to lithium?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: compare the size of the atoms and their first ionization energies from cesium up the group to lithium, and connect how easily each atom loses its single valence electron with how readily the metal is oxidized.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: for (a) and (c), place the elements in the periodic table and use the trends in size and ionization energy across a period and down a group; for (b), compare how strongly each metal holds its valence electrons, recalling what the text says of the group 2 metals with the highest ionization energies; for (d) and (e), compare the numbers of electrons held by the same or by nearly the same nuclear charge.

exercises.prompt: Sodium chloride and strontium chloride are both white solids. How could you distinguish one from the other?

answer.solution: The possible ways of distinguishing between the two include infrared spectroscopy by comparison of known compounds, a flame test that gives the characteristic yellow color for sodium (strontium has a red flame), or comparison of their solubilities in water. At 20 °C, NaCl dissolves to the extent of $\frac{\text{35.7 g}}{\text{100 mL}}$ compared with $\frac{\text{53.8 g}}{\text{100 mL}}$ for SrCl<sub>2</sub>. Heating to 100 °C provides an easy test, since the solubility of NaCl is $\frac{\text{39.12 g}}{\text{100 mL}},$ but that of SrCl<sub>2</sub> is $\frac{\text{100.8 g}}{\text{100 mL}}.$ Density determination on a solid is sometimes difficult, but there is enough difference (2.165 g/mL NaCl and 3.052 g/mL SrCl<sub>2</sub>) that this method would be viable and perhaps the easiest and least expensive test to perform.

exercises.prompt: Does metallic tin react with HCl?

answer.solution: Yes, tin reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen gas.

exercises.prompt: What is tin pest, also known as tin disease?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: recall the two common allotropes of tin and the temperature, 13.2 °C, above which white tin is the stable form; describe what happens to a tin article in a long cold spell, and why the change spreads from the spot where it starts.

exercises.prompt: Compare the nature of the bonds in PbCl<sub>2</sub> to that of the bonds in PbCl<sub>4</sub>.

answer.solution: In PbCl<sub>2</sub>, the bonding is ionic, as indicated by its melting point of 501 °C. In PbCl<sub>4</sub>, the bonding is covalent, as evidenced by it being an unstable liquid at room temperature.

exercises.prompt: Is the reaction of rubidium with water more or less vigorous than that of sodium? How does the rate of reaction of magnesium compare?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: use the trend in reactivity down group 1 that follows from the ionization energies, then place magnesium, an alkaline earth metal of the same period as sodium, against the alkali metals, recalling what passivation and Figure 18.6 show about magnesium in water.
